items.title: India's Biggest Digital Trust Provider Just Collapsed: The eMudhra Crisis!
items.summary: Trust is the only currency in cybersecurity—and India’s largest digital trust provider just lost it. eMudhra has officially announced its exit from the global SSL/TLS certificate business following a catastrophic key-generation failure. Due to a critical error in April, the company generated incredibly weak P-384 private keys that were just single- and double-digit numbers—allowing researchers to crack them in less than a second. Had malicious actors found this vulnerability first, they could have forged fake website certificates to impersonate legitimate banks and portals. Facing bans from Google, Mozilla, and Apple, eMudhra is retreating to focus on its domestic eSign services. Are global browsers relying too much on a certificate authority system prone to human error? Sound off in the comments! 📌 Subscribe to Front Page by AIM Network: Think AI. items.title: Data Centers Aren't Wasting Your Water
items.summary: In episode 1037 of the SuperDataScience podcast, Jon Krohn discusses with Dr. Richard Socher, CEO of Recursive whether AI data centers are really using up all our water. Socher calls the idea that data centers steam their water back into the atmosphere a lie, explaining that almost all data centers today are closed water systems. He encourages talking to the communities around them, in the hope that they respond to the facts, which are mostly positive.

items.title: Microsoft's New AI Diagnoses Patients 2x Better Than Human Doctors!
items.summary: Microsoft has just unveiled a massive breakthrough in medical AI. Unlike standard symptom search engines that try to read a patient's entire file at once, Microsoft’s new sequential orchestrator model acts like a panel of clinical experts—asking questions, ordering tests, and updating hypotheses step-by-step. Published this Thursday in Science, the results show this new AI system is more than twice as accurate at determining correct diagnoses than human general physicians using textbooks and the internet. The system also outperformed doctors when tested on real-world ER admission scenarios and proved to be more cost-efficient by eliminating unnecessary lab tests. Next stop?
